sections.title: Holmes on Irene Adler and Watson's deductions

moments.summary: Watson narrates Holmes's cold, unemotional regard for Irene Adler as the only woman in his mind; a quiet study of a reasoner's mind.
Watson, married and busy, sees Holmes in Baker Street among old books and drug haze; he passes the familiar door one evening and glimpses Holmes pacing the lit room.
Holmes in his rooms by the fire greets Watson, deduces his marriage and wet walk from his shoe and servant, and explains the reasoning while gesturing at Watson's clothing.
Watson laughs at the ease of Holmes's deductions, holding a cigarette-smoking Holmes and his puzzled friend in the room.

sections.title: Observation versus seeing; the pink notepaper arrives

moments.summary: Holmes quizzes Watson on the seventeen steps to the room, then tosses him the thick pink notepaper that came by post.

sections.title: The notepaper traced to Bohemia

moments.summary: Watson reads the undated, unsigned note warning of a masked visitor at a quarter to eight.
Watson examines the paper against the light, finds woven watermarks, and Holmes lifts the gazetteer.
Holmes reads the Egria entry aloud, triumphant with a blue cloud of smoke; the note's German syntax points to a German writer, and a brougham outside announces the caller.

sections.title: The brougham arrives and the visitor is awaited

moments.summary: The pair of horses and brougham pull up outside; Holmes insists Watson stay, and a heavy tread halts at the door before the tap.

sections.title: The masked visitor unmasked as the King

moments.summary: A giant masked man in rich furs and a flaming beryl brooch enters, introduces himself as Count Von Kramm, and Holmes keeps Watson present.
The visitor binds them to secrecy and names the House of Ormstein; Holmes lounges, eyes closed, while the giant grows impatient.
The masked man tears off his mask and admits he is the King; Holmes names him Wilhelm von Ormstein and Watson looks up Irene Adler in the index.

sections.title: The King explains the Irene Adler photograph

moments.summary: Holmes recites Irene Adler's biography and questions the King about any marriage or papers, learning there were only letters and a photograph.
A quick-fire exchange: forgery, stolen note-paper, the King's seal and photograph; five failed attempts to recover it, and the King pleads for help.

sections.title: Payment and terms; the King departs

moments.summary: Holmes learns Irene plans to send the photograph to the King's fiancee, Clotilde, on Monday; the King is distraught and sits still as Holmes questions him.
Holmes asks the King to stay in London, takes a chamois bag of gold and notes and a receipt, learns Briony Lodge's address, and sees the King off into the street.

sections.title: Holmes's morning reconnaissance and the wedding

moments.summary: Watson waits at Baker Street at three; at four a drunken groom in side-whiskers stumbles in, and Holmes, changed back, laughs by the fire.
Holmes describes watching Briony Lodge disguised as a groom, the mews gossip about Irene, and her visitor Godfrey Norton, a lawyer.
Norton arrives in a hansom, rushes inside, emerges pulling out his watch and ordering the cabman to race to a church.
Irene hurries from the house in a landau, cries for St. Monica's, and Holmes hails a cab to follow.
Inside the church, Norton grabs Holmes as a witness, and Holmes is pressed into vouching for the marriage of Irene and Norton.

sections.title: Holmes's plan and his instructions to Watson

moments.summary: The couple part ways outside; Irene says she will drive in the park at five; Holmes sits down to cold beef and asks for Watson's help.
Holmes explains that Watson must do nothing but watch from the window and throw the signal rocket when he raises his hand, then cry fire.

sections.title: Holmes's disguise and the approach to Briony Lodge

moments.summary: Holmes details the signal rocket and Watson's role in detail and then goes to change for his new role.
Holmes emerges as a benevolent Nonconformist clergyman and the two set out, arriving in Serpentine Avenue at dusk with loiterers around.

sections.title: Waiting outside; Irene Adler returns and the staged quarrel

moments.summary: Holmes and Watson pace before Briony Lodge reasoning about where the photograph is hidden; the landau arrives and Holmes prepares his plan.
A staged scuffle erupts at the carriage door; Holmes is struck down with red paint on his face while Irene stands on the steps.

sections.title: Holmes carried in; the false fire alarm

moments.summary: Holmes is carried into the sitting-room on a sofa while Irene tends him; Watson, ashamed, hardens his heart by the window.
Holmes raises his hand and Watson throws the rocket in with a cry of fire; the room fills with smoke and the crowd shouts, and Watson escapes to the corner.

sections.title: Holmes explains the trick; the greeting in the street

moments.summary: Walking away with Holmes, he explains the trick: the staged fall, the fire alarm, and how Irene rushed to the hidden panel and the photograph.
Holmes plans to call with the King next morning; at Baker Street a slim youth in an ulster calls out Holmes's name in the dim street.

sections.title: Next morning: the King arrives and they set off

moments.summary: Next morning the King bursts in at breakfast; the three drive off in the brougham, and Holmes says Irene has married Norton.

sections.title: Briony Lodge deserted; the servant's news

moments.summary: The King laments that Irene was not of his station; the brougham stops at Serpentine Avenue and the King broods silently.
An elderly servant on the steps watches them and reports that her mistress has fled to the Continent with her husband that morning.

sections.title: Irene's letter, the photograph, and the close

moments.summary: The drawing-room is ransacked; Holmes tears open a sliding shutter and pulls out the photograph and a letter addressed to himself.
Irene's letter is read aloud: she saw through Holmes's disguise and fled, keeping the photograph as safeguard and signing herself Irene Norton, nee Adler.
The King praises Irene; Holmes refuses the emerald ring and asks for the photograph itself, and the two men leave the King in the drawing-room closing the scandal.

sections.title: Wilson introduced to Holmes

moments.summary: Watson enters Holmes's room to find Holmes deep in talk with a stout, red-haired elderly man, Mr. Wilson, and Holmes pulls Watson inside to stay.
Holmes, fingertips together, invites Watson to sit on the settee and asks Wilson to restart his story while Wilson sits with the newspaper on his knee.

sections.title: Holmes reads Wilson's bearing

moments.summary: Watson studies Wilson's shabby appearance: baggy checked trousers, unbuttoned frock-coat, brassy Albert chain, frayed top-hat and faded overcoat on a chair.
Holmes lists his deductions about Wilson's manual labour, snuff and Freemasonry while Wilson leans forward, startled, the paper in his hand.
Holmes explains the tattoo of a fish and the Chinese coin on the watch-chain, and Wilson laughs heavily as Holmes pauses over the advertisement.

sections.title: The advertisement and Wilson's shop

moments.summary: Wilson's thick red finger points to the newspaper advertisement, which Watson reads aloud in a bewildered voice while Holmes chuckles and wriggles in his chair.
Wilson describes his small pawnbroker's shop in Coburg Square and his assistant Vincent Spaulding, who works for half wages and takes photographs.

sections.title: Spaulding's tip and the crowd at Pope's Court

moments.summary: Wilson recounts Spaulding coming down to the shop with the newspaper, eager that his hair might change colour, and explaining the League of the Red-headed Men.
Wilson and Spaulding push through a vast crowd of red-headed men thronging Fleet Street and Pope's Court, a sight like a coster's orange barrow.

sections.title: Hiring interview with Duncan Ross

moments.summary: In the small office, the red-headed manager Duncan Ross inspects Wilson's hair closely, tugs it hard, and then shouts from the window that the vacancy is filled.
Ross questions whether Wilson is married, frowns at his bachelorhood, then agrees and sets the hours from ten to two while Spaulding offers to mind the shop.
Ross explains the pay and the rule of never leaving the building, then sets Wilson copying the Encyclopaedia Britannica at a table in the office.

sections.title: Eight weeks of copying

moments.summary: Wilson, doubting the scheme, returns the next morning with ink, pen and foolscap, finds the office ready, and copies entries day after day for eight weeks.

sections.title: The League dissolved; Wilson's client inquiries

moments.summary: Wilson shows a cardboard notice on the locked office door announcing the League is dissolved, and Holmes and Watson burst into laughter.
Wilson describes his fruitless search: the landlord, the artificial knee-cap factory, and Holmes questions him about Spaulding's appearance and ears.

sections.title: Questioning Wilson about Spaulding

moments.summary: Holmes sits up in excitement at the pierced ears while Wilson confirms Spaulding has been with him a month and has never missed a morning, and Holmes promises an opinion by Monday.

sections.title: Holmes examines Saxe-Coburg Square

moments.summary: Holmes sits curled in his armchair smoking a black clay pipe in silence, then springs up and proposes they go to the afternoon concert.
Holmes stops before the shabby pawnbroker's on Saxe-Coburg Square, thumps the pavement with his stick, and speaks with the bright young assistant at the door.
Holmes and Watson walk away from the square, with Holmes saying he noticed the knees of the assistant's trousers and calling them spies in enemy country.
On the busy main road behind the square, Holmes names the shops in order at the corner before leading Watson off for a sandwich and coffee.

sections.title: Afternoon concert and plans for the night

moments.summary: Holmes sits rapt in the stalls at St. James's Hall, gently waving his fingers to German music, his face serene and dreamy.
As they emerge from the concert hall, Holmes tells Watson to meet him at Baker Street at ten armed with his revolver, promising danger and a serious crime.

sections.title: Gathering the party at Baker Street

moments.summary: Watson rides home puzzling over the plan, then crosses the Park and arrives at Baker Street to find Holmes talking with Peter Jones and Merryweather.
Holmes introduces Jones of Scotland Yard and Merryweather, the bank director, and Jones describes John Clay, the criminal they hope to catch.

sections.title: The bank cellar stakeout

moments.summary: In a cab rattling through gaslit streets, Holmes hums tunes and remarks that Merryweather is a bank director and Jones brave but dim.
Merryweather leads the party through a side door, down winding stone steps and dark passages into a vast bank cellar piled with crates, where he knocks the floor and Holmes scolds him.
Holmes examines the cracks in the flagstones with a lens and explains the bank holds French gold in the cellar, while Merryweather perches on a crate.
Holmes assigns hiding places behind crates, shutters the lantern into total darkness, and the men wait silently for the robbers.

sections.title: Clay breaks through and is captured

moments.summary: In the black vault Watson waits, his nerves tense, until a glint of light appears in a crack and a pale hand emerges from the floor.
A stone turns over and a boyish red-haired man climbs through the hole with a lantern, hauling up a companion, until Holmes seizes him and knocks a revolver from John Clay's wrist.
Holmes and Clay trade calm remarks while Jones snaps on the handcuffs and reports the men waiting at the door.
Clay demands polite address and a royal courtesy, and Jones mockingly leads him upstairs toward a cab as Clay bows and walks off serenely.

sections.title: Explanation at Baker Street

moments.summary: Merryweather thanks Holmes effusively as they leave the cellar, and Holmes says he will expect the bank to refund his expenses.
At Baker Street in the early morning, Holmes sits with whisky and soda explaining to Watson how he reasoned out the scheme from the cellar and the assistant's knees.
Watson praises the chain of reasoning, Holmes yawns and speaks of escaping the commonplace, quoting Flaubert, as they sit by the fire at Baker Street.

sections.title: Fireside talk on life and fiction

moments.summary: Holmes and the narrator sit by the fire at Baker Street, Holmes gesturing toward the window as he speaks of life's strangeness while the narrator holds up the morning paper.
Holmes takes the paper and then displays his jewelled snuffbox and ring, while the narrator asks about his current cases with the window blinds parted behind him.

sections.title: Arrival of Miss Sutherland

moments.summary: Seen from the window, a large woman in a fur boa and red-feathered hat hesitates on the pavement opposite before hurrying across the road toward the door.
Miss Mary Sutherland, a broad-faced woman in a heavy hat, is shown into the room by the boy in buttons and sits in an armchair while Holmes studies her closely.
Mary sits anxiously in the armchair explaining her stepfather and her small income while Holmes, fingertips together, listens intently.

sections.title: Mary's courtship by Hosmer Angel

moments.summary: Mary, flushing and picking at her jacket fringe, recounts meeting Hosmer Angel at the gasfitters' ball while Holmes and Watson listen.
Mary describes the engagement and the couple's odd letter arrangements while Holmes questions her about the shy, tinted-glasses suitor.

sections.title: The wedding morning and the vanished bridegroom

moments.summary: Mary recounts Angel's proposal to marry before her stepfather returns, and the failed letter to Bordeaux, as Holmes listens by the fire.
At the church door of St. Saviour's, Mary stands beside an empty four-wheeler whose cabman stares into its vacant interior, having seen Angel get in.
Mary sits sobbing into a handkerchief in her muff while Holmes stands near the fireplace, her parents' reactions discussed in the room.

sections.title: Holmes takes the case; Mary departs

moments.summary: Holmes rises and comforts Mary, handing her the advertisement slip and letters, as she leaves the room with the narrator watching.

sections.title: Holmes reads the clues; letters sent

moments.summary: Holmes sits back with his clay pipe and a cloud of smoke while Watson reads the advertisement's description of the missing man aloud.
Holmes shows Watson the typewritten letters and signatures on the desk, then writes his letters, while Watson leaves him puffing his pipe.

sections.title: Windibank arrives

moments.summary: Holmes sits half-asleep in his armchair amid bottles and test-tubes of chemical apparatus as Watson enters and asks about the case.
James Windibank, a sallow middle-aged man in a shiny top-hat, sidles into the room and sits in the nearest chair as Holmes greets him.

sections.title: Confrontation and the unmasking

moments.summary: Holmes lays four typewritten letters on the table beside a magnifying lens while Windibank sits tense, dropping his gloves and rising to leave.
Holmes locks the door and Windibank, pale and sweating, collapses into a chair as Holmes faces him across the room.
Holmes paces by the mantelpiece reciting the stepfather's scheme while Windibank rises sneering, then bolts down the stairs as Holmes reaches for a hunting crop.

sections.title: Holmes explains his reasoning

moments.summary: Holmes laughs and settles back into his chair while Watson asks about his reasoning, with the room still and the hunting crop lying on the table.

sections.title: Telegram and departure from London

moments.summary: Watson and his wife at the breakfast table, a maid handing over a telegram while the wife looks across at him.
Watson hesitates over his workload, his wife urges him to go, and he packs; then at Paddington Station Holmes paces the platform in his grey cloak and cap.

sections.title: Holmes explains the case on the train

moments.summary: Inside a railway carriage Holmes tosses a huge ball of newspapers onto the rack while Watson looks on, and Holmes begins explaining the case.
Holmes lays out the background of the Boscombe Valley families, Turner and McCarthy, in the carriage as the countryside passes.
Holmes recounts the movements of McCarthy on the afternoon of the killing and the quarrel witnessed by the young girl near the pool.
Watson and Holmes debate the damning circumstantial evidence, Holmes pointing out that the room's window is on the right.
Holmes demonstrates his observational powers by pointing out Watson's uneven shaving on the left side, then mentions the arrest remark.
Holmes and Watson discuss the young man's reaction to arrest and his claims of innocence, and Holmes offers the local newspaper.

sections.title: James McCarthy's inquest statement

moments.summary: Watson settles in the carriage corner with the newspaper, reading young McCarthy's statement of the events at the pool.
In the inquest room the coroner presses James McCarthy, who stands uneasily before the jury and refuses to explain the quarrel.
The questioning turns to the vanished grey cloth James glimpsed near the body, the jury and coroner pressing him on its disappearance.

sections.title: Discussion of the coroner's remarks

moments.summary: Watson reflects on the coroner's damning remarks while Holmes reclines on the seat, arguing the young man's account may be true.

sections.title: Arrival at Ross and meeting Lestrade

moments.summary: Holmes and Watson step off the train at Ross, where Lestrade waits in his rustic dustcoat, and they head to the Hereford Arms.
At the hotel tea table Holmes comments on the barometer and cigarettes while Lestrade, puzzled, dismisses the case as plain.

sections.title: Alice Turner's visit to the hotel

moments.summary: Alice Turner bursts into the hotel room, her violet eyes bright, insisting that James is innocent and appealing to Holmes.
Alice explains the quarrels over her marriage to James and speaks of her ailing father, Lestrade shrugging as Holmes questions her.
Holmes gets Alice's answers about the Victorian gold mines, then she leaves, and Holmes arranges to visit the prison at Hereford.

sections.title: Watson alone at the hotel

moments.summary: Watson lies on the sofa at the hotel with a novel, his mind turning over the injuries, the rat and the grey cloth.

sections.title: Holmes's visit to James and his report

moments.summary: Holmes returns alone in the evening and reports his talk with James, explaining the Bristol marriage and the crucial clues of the cry and the appointment.

sections.title: Morning journey to Hatherley Farm and Lestrade's views

moments.summary: Next morning Lestrade drives Holmes and Watson out, reporting Turner's illness, and Holmes questions McCarthy's generosity and marriage plans.
Lestrade and Holmes spar over facts and theories in the carriage as the Hatherley Farm comes into view.

sections.title: Examining the farm, the pool and the tracks

moments.summary: At Hatherley Farm the maid shows the boots of the father and son, which Holmes measures carefully in the yard.
Holmes, transformed by the scent, strides along the marshy track through the meadows with Lestrade and Watson trailing behind.
At the Boscombe Pool Holmes questions Lestrade about his raking of the water while examining the trampled grass by the reeds.
Holmes crawls on his waterproof reading footprints, then under a great beech tree gathers ash and examines the bark with his lens.

sections.title: Holmes leaves the stone and speaks with Lestrade

moments.summary: Holmes leaves the wood, speaks of visiting the lodge, and rejoins the cab carrying a stone from the wood.
Holmes hands Lestrade the stone and describes the murderer's build, limp, boots and cigar habits, while Lestrade remains skeptical.
Holmes and Lestrade exchange terse words on the unfinished case, and Holmes leaves Lestrade at his lodgings.

sections.title: Holmes's deductions at the hotel

moments.summary: Back at the hotel over the lunch cloth, Holmes sits in his chair and begins expounding the 'Cooee' signal and its Australian meaning.
Holmes spreads a map of Victoria on the table, revealing the word Ballarat in the dying man's mumbled rat reference.
Holmes explains how he deduced the murderer's height, lameness and boots from the footprints, with Watson listening intently.
Holmes lays out the left-handedness, the Indian cigar ash and the blunt pen-knife, and Watson names Turner just as the waiter announces a visitor.

sections.title: John Turner's visit and the setting of his confession

moments.summary: John Turner enters the sitting room, a gaunt, bluish-lipped old man leaning on his limp, and sinks onto the sofa as Holmes greets him.
Turner covers his face in despair as Holmes acknowledges he knows about McCarthy, and the old man vows he would have spoken at the Assizes.
Holmes sits at the table with pen and paper preparing to take down Turner's confession, Watson present as witness.

sections.title: Turner's confession and the acquittal

moments.summary: Turner begins his confession, describing himself as a young highwayman known as Black Jack of Ballarat, with Holmes writing beside him.
Turner recounts the gold convoy robbery and then McCarthy accosting him in Regent Street, the old man's voice trembling as he speaks.
Turner tells of McCarthy's grip on him and the fatal meeting at the pool, where he strikes McCarthy down behind a tree.
Turner signs the statement, Holmes promises his secret will be kept, and the old man shuffles slowly out of the room.
Holmes and Watson sit in silence after the visitor leaves, and the story closes with James's acquittal at the Assizes.

sections.title: A stormy night and an unexpected visitor

moments.summary: Watson looks back on his notes of cases from the 1880s and describes the stormy autumn evening in Baker Street, with Holmes cross-indexing records by one side of the fire and Watson reading at the other.
A bell rings in the storm; Holmes turns the lamp toward the empty chair as a pale, well-dressed young man with a streaming umbrella enters and introduces himself as John Openshaw.

sections.title: Openshaw introduces his family

moments.summary: Openshaw pulls his chair near the fire, his wet feet toward the blaze, and begins to explain his family's mysterious history while Holmes listens attentively.

sections.title: Colonel Elias Openshaw's life and death

moments.summary: Openshaw describes his father's bicycle-tyre business and his uncle Elias, a fierce, brandy-drinking planter back from America, living in a Sussex house near Horsham with the young boy as his household deputy.
At breakfast the colonel opens a letter from Pondicherry; five dried orange pips fall onto his plate, and he collapses in terror, shrieking K.K.K. and ordering a fire lit in his room.

Inside the colonel's room a fire burns and the open brass box, marked K.K.K., stands beside black ash, while the lawyer Fordham witnesses his will; later the colonel is found drowned in a green-scummed pool.

sections.title: The attic box and the colonel's will

moments.summary: Holmes questions Openshaw about dates, and Openshaw reports the attic's contents: the brass box with its label and the sorted papers about the colonel's American life.

sections.title: The father's letter and death

moments.summary: At the breakfast table in January 1885 Openshaw's father opens an envelope with orange pips and K.K.K. written inside, reads the instruction to put the papers on the sundial, and looks baffled and scared.
Father and son argue over the Dundee-postmarked letter; the father refuses to involve the police and dismisses the warning as nonsense.
Openshaw describes his father's fatal fall into a chalk-pit on the way back from Fareham, and his own unease as he lives on at Horsham.

sections.title: Openshaw's second warning and the police

moments.summary: Openshaw lays a new envelope with five orange pips on the table in Baker Street, showing the London postmark and the K.K.K. warning, and Holmes asks what he has done.
Openshaw confesses helplessness, reports that the police dismissed his story, and produces a torn blue-tinted diary page from the colonel's room, which Holmes studies by lamplight.

sections.title: The diary page and Holmes's instructions

moments.summary: Holmes and Watson bend over the diary page headed March 1869, reading its cryptic entries about Hudson, the pips sent to McCauley, Paramore and John Swain, and who cleared.
Holmes tells Openshaw to put the surviving page into the brass box with a note, then set the box out on the sundial immediately.

sections.title: Openshaw departs and Holmes reflects

moments.summary: Holmes urges Openshaw to act at once and to take care on the streets, while Openshaw stands with his overcoat on, ready to leave for the London train.
Openshaw declares he is armed and says goodbye; Holmes promises to work on the case, and the storm outside seems to swallow the strange visit.
Holmes sits silently smoking by the fire, then begins a lecture to Watson on the ideal reasoner and the usefulness of stored knowledge.

sections.title: Holmes explains the K.K.K. and the ship

moments.summary: Holmes and Watson recall Watson's old list of Holmes's accomplishments, then Holmes deduces from the postmarks that the senders travel by sailing ship, with the delay implying the distance.
Holmes explains that the K.K.K. is a secret society, reads from the encyclopaedia about the Ku Klux Klan and its warnings of orange pips, and predicts the danger to Openshaw is urgent.

sections.title: The news of Openshaw's death

moments.summary: At breakfast the next morning Holmes prepares to leave for the City while Watson waits, having just noticed a newspaper heading that chills him.

Watson reads the newspaper report of Openshaw's body pulled from the river near Waterloo Bridge, and Holmes, pale and shaken, paces the room with a vow of revenge; that evening he returns hungry and worn.

sections.title: The trap for the Lone Star

moments.summary: Holmes tears an orange, squeezes out five pips into an envelope marked S.H. for J.O., and addresses it to Captain James Calhoun of the barque Lone Star at Savannah.
Holmes lays out his paper of dates and names, explaining how he traced the Lone Star from Pondicherry and Dundee to London and why its American crew are now to be arrested for murder.

stories.name: The Adventure Of The Blue Carbuncle

sections.start_ref: The Adventure Of The Blue Carbuncle ¶1
sections.end_ref: The Adventure Of The Blue Carbuncle ¶8
sections.title: Holmes examines the battered hat
sections.division_name: The Adventure Of The Blue Carbuncle

moments.summary: Watson enters Holmes's sitting room to find him lounging on a sofa in a purple dressing-gown, with a pipe-rack and crumpled newspapers nearby and a battered old hat hanging from a chair, examined with a lens and forceps.
Holmes, seated by the fire, waves Watson toward the armchair as he explains the hat is a trivial matter tied to Peterson the commissionaire, whose name is mentioned as the bearer of the trophy.

sections.start_ref: The Adventure Of The Blue Carbuncle ¶9
sections.end_ref: The Adventure Of The Blue Carbuncle ¶28
sections.title: Peterson's account of the hat and goose
sections.division_name: The Adventure Of The Blue Carbuncle

moments.summary: Holmes gestures at the battered hat on the chair while Watson looks on, and then recounts Peterson's Christmas morning encounter on Tottenham Court Road, where a stranger dropped a goose and fled.

Holmes and Watson discuss the card on the goose and the initials inside the hat, with the men stood in the room; Holmes explains why the owner was not easily traced and that the hat and goose were brought to him.
Watson turns the hat over with a rueful look, Holmes handing it back and then picking it up with an introspective gaze as he begins to reason aloud about its owner.

sections.start_ref: The Adventure Of The Blue Carbuncle ¶29
sections.end_ref: The Adventure Of The Blue Carbuncle ¶46
sections.title: Holmes deduces the owner's character from the hat
sections.division_name: The Adventure Of The Blue Carbuncle

moments.summary: Holmes, holding the hat, lists his inferences about the owner's middle age, grizzled hair, and lack of gas lighting as Watson protests in the room.
Holmes puts the hat on his own head, where it settles over his nose, and explains that its size reveals intellect and its age and quality reveal the owner's decline.
Holmes points to the hat-securer and the ink-smeared stains as signs of foresight and self-respect, then examines the lining under the lens for hair-ends and lime-cream.
Holmes deduces the wife's lost affection from the unbrushed hat and the tallow stains, telling Watson of the owner walking upstairs with a candle while Watson sits listening.

sections.start_ref: The Adventure Of The Blue Carbuncle ¶47
sections.end_ref: The Adventure Of The Blue Carbuncle ¶58
sections.title: Peterson returns with the blue stone
sections.division_name: The Adventure Of The Blue Carbuncle

moments.summary: Watson remarks that the whole deduction seems a waste of energy with no crime; Holmes opens his mouth to reply as Peterson bursts into the room, flushed and astonished.
Peterson, gasping, holds out his palm to Holmes, who sits up on the sofa, revealing a brilliant blue stone found in the goose's crop.
Holmes sits up with a whistle and identifies the stone as the Countess of Morcar's blue carbuncle, with Peterson sinking into a chair and staring at both men.

sections.start_ref: The Adventure Of The Blue Carbuncle ¶59
sections.end_ref: The Adventure Of The Blue Carbuncle ¶70
sections.title: The Hotel Cosmopolitan theft and the advertisement
sections.division_name: The Adventure Of The Blue Carbuncle

moments.summary: Holmes rummages through newspapers and reads aloud the police-court report of the Hotel Cosmopolitan jewel robbery, with Watson listening in the room.
Holmes takes a pencil and slip of paper and composes an advertisement for Henry Baker to claim the goose and hat, explaining its wording to Watson.
Holmes sends Peterson off with the advertisement to the newspapers and asks him to buy a replacement goose, while Holmes keeps the stone.

sections.start_ref: The Adventure Of The Blue Carbuncle ¶71
sections.end_ref: The Adventure Of The Blue Carbuncle ¶78
sections.title: Holmes examines the stone's history
sections.division_name: The Adventure Of The Blue Carbuncle

moments.summary: Holmes holds the blue stone up to the lamplight in his room, describing its sinister history as a carbuncle with a trail of crimes behind it.
Watson asks whether Horner and Baker are innocent, Holmes answers guardedly, and Watson agrees to return at the appointed hour for the evening.

sections.start_ref: The Adventure Of The Blue Carbuncle ¶79
sections.end_ref: The Adventure Of The Blue Carbuncle ¶94
sections.title: Henry Baker collects his hat and is sent away with a goose
sections.division_name: The Adventure Of The Blue Carbuncle

moments.summary: Holmes proposes examining the woodcock's crop; Watson arrives at Baker Street near six-thirty and sees a tall man in a Scotch bonnet waiting in the light from the fanlight.
Holmes greets Henry Baker warmly and seats him by the fire; Baker, a large grizzled man with a pointed beard, confirms the hat is his and explains he did not advertise.
Holmes says they ate the first goose and offers a replacement; Baker accepts the new bird and explains the goose club at the Alpha Inn before bowing and striding off.

sections.start_ref: The Adventure Of The Blue Carbuncle ¶95
sections.end_ref: The Adventure Of The Blue Carbuncle ¶108
sections.title: Holmes and Watson at the Alpha Inn
sections.division_name: The Adventure Of The Blue Carbuncle

moments.summary: Holmes, with Watson, dismisses Baker as innocent and suggests turning dinner into supper to follow the clue while it is hot.
Holmes and Watson walk through the cold street, pulling on ulsters and cravats, their breath steaming in the starlight as they pass the doctors' quarter toward Bloomsbury.
In the private bar of the Alpha Inn, Holmes and Watson drink beer with the ruddy-faced landlord, who admits the geese came from a salesman in Covent Garden.

sections.start_ref: The Adventure Of The Blue Carbuncle ¶109
sections.end_ref: The Adventure Of The Blue Carbuncle ¶151
sections.title: Breckinridge's ledger and the wager
sections.division_name: The Adventure Of The Blue Carbuncle

moments.summary: Holmes tells Watson they must follow the line of investigation to the end, and they cross Holborn and Covent Garden to the Breckinridge stall, where a horsey salesman is helping a boy shutter it.
Holmes greets the salesman at the bare marble slabs and asks about the geese, while the salesman eyes him suspiciously under the gas-flare.
The salesman grows angry and argues with Holmes over whether the geese were country or town bred, the two haggling over a wager at the stall.
The boy brings the ledgers beneath the hanging lamp and the salesman shows Holmes the supplier entries, the greasy ledger open between them.
Holmes throws down a sovereign and turns away chagrined, then laughs under a lamp-post, explaining how he drew the salesman out by a bet.

sections.start_ref: The Adventure Of The Blue Carbuncle ¶152
sections.end_ref: The Adventure Of The Blue Carbuncle ¶172
sections.title: The little man follows Holmes; the cab to Baker Street
sections.division_name: The Adventure Of The Blue Carbuncle

moments.summary: A loud hubbub erupts at the stall as a rat-faced little man stands in the lamplight while Breckinridge shakes his fists at him.
Breckinridge shouts that he has had enough of the geese and sets his dog at the rat-faced man, who flees into the darkness.
Holmes strides through the market crowd, overtakes the little man, and reveals that he knows of the geese and their path, startling him into a trembling plea.
Holmes hails a four-wheeler and coaxes the man, who gives his name as James Ryder, into the cab for the ride back to Baker Street.
Ryder sits in the basket-chair in the Baker Street sitting room, watched by Holmes, who puts on his slippers and asks about the white goose.

sections.start_ref: The Adventure Of The Blue Carbuncle ¶173
sections.end_ref: The Adventure Of The Blue Carbuncle ¶200
sections.title: Ryder confesses and tells of the stone in the goose
sections.division_name: The Adventure Of The Blue Carbuncle

moments.summary: Holmes says the white goose with a barred tail came to him and laid a blue egg after it was dead, offering to show Ryder the bird's remains.
Ryder staggers to his feet and grips the mantelpiece as Holmes holds up the blue carbuncle, which glitters coldly in the lamplight; Holmes steadies him.
Ryder, pale and in the basket-chair, admits Catherine Cusack told him of the stone, while Holmes lays out how he framed Horner for the theft.
Ryder throws himself onto the rug and clutches Holmes's knees, pleading for mercy for his father and mother, while Holmes sternly tells him to get back into his chair.
Holmes demands the truth of how the stone entered the goose, and Ryder begins to recount his flight to his sister's house in Brixton Road.
Ryder describes forcing the stone down the throat of a white barred-tailed goose in the yard while his sister Maggie looks on, and then taking the bird away to Kilburn.

sections.start_ref: The Adventure Of The Blue Carbuncle ¶201
sections.end_ref: The Adventure Of The Blue Carbuncle ¶214
sections.title: Ryder's search for the goose and Holmes's release of him
sections.division_name: The Adventure Of The Blue Carbuncle

moments.summary: Ryder finds the yard empty, learns the birds went to Breckinridge, and sobs with his face in his hands in the Baker Street room.
After a long silence, Holmes rises and throws open the door, telling Ryder to get out, and the man rushes down the stairs into the street.
Holmes lights his clay pipe and explains to Watson why he lets Ryder go, then reaches for the bell to begin the next investigation, which will also feature a bird.

stories.name: The Adventure Of The Speckled Band

sections.start_ref: The Adventure Of The Speckled Band ¶1
sections.end_ref: The Adventure Of The Speckled Band ¶8
sections.title: Helen's early-morning visit to Baker Street
sections.division_name: The Adventure Of The Speckled Band

moments.summary: A narrator-writer reflects in an ordinary room about his many cases with Holmes; no visual action, only a writer at a desk with notes.
Holmes, fully dressed, stands at the bedside of a sleepy Watson at a quarter past seven; later in the sitting-room a veiled woman in black sits by the fire while Holmes greets her and orders coffee.

sections.start_ref: The Adventure Of The Speckled Band ¶9
sections.end_ref: The Adventure Of The Speckled Band ¶19
sections.title: Helen's arrival and the reason for coming
sections.division_name: The Adventure Of The Speckled Band

moments.summary: Helen Stoner, pale and shivering in her black veil, shifts seats by the fire as Holmes reads her mud-spattered sleeve and return ticket.
Helen pleads for help while Holmes takes a small case-book from his desk and consults it.

sections.start_ref: The Adventure Of The Speckled Band ¶20
sections.end_ref: The Adventure Of The Speckled Band ¶34
sections.title: Helen describes her family and the Roylott history
sections.division_name: The Adventure Of The Speckled Band

moments.summary: Helen, seated by the fire, introduces herself and her stepfather's family history while Holmes listens with eyes half-closed; the scene is the sitting-room.
Helen describes her dead twin sister and the layout of the bedrooms, Holmes leaning back attentively in the sitting-room.

sections.start_ref: The Adventure Of The Speckled Band ¶35
sections.end_ref: The Adventure Of The Speckled Band ¶49
sections.title: Julia's account of the night whistle
sections.division_name: The Adventure Of The Speckled Band

moments.summary: Helen and Julia stand at Helen's bedroom door at night, Julia asking about a strange whistle before hurrying off and locking her door.
Holmes questions Helen in the sitting-room about the habit of locking doors because of the cheetah and baboon.

sections.start_ref: The Adventure Of The Speckled Band ¶50
sections.end_ref: The Adventure Of The Speckled Band ¶57
sections.title: Julia's death and the coroner's findings
sections.division_name: The Adventure Of The Speckled Band

moments.summary: Helen, in a wild storm, rushes into the corridor as her sister Julia staggers from her unlocked door, collapsing in terror and gasping about the speckled band.
In the sitting-room Holmes presses Helen on the whistle and the charred match, while the inquest findings are discussed.

sections.start_ref: The Adventure Of The Speckled Band ¶58
sections.end_ref: The Adventure Of The Speckled Band ¶71
sections.title: Julia's engagement, Helen's new room and the wrist marks
sections.division_name: The Adventure Of The Speckled Band

moments.summary: Holmes and Helen talk over the coroner's verdict and the phrase about a band, Holmes shaking his head by the fire.
Helen explains her engagement and the new bedroom where she now sleeps; Holmes notes she is hiding something.

sections.start_ref: The Adventure Of The Speckled Band ¶72
sections.end_ref: The Adventure Of The Speckled Band ¶83
sections.title: The bruises revealed and the plan to visit Stoke Moran
sections.division_name: The Adventure Of The Speckled Band

moments.summary: Holmes lifts the black lace from Helen's wrist to reveal five livid finger-marks while she colours and covers them.
Holmes arranges with Helen to visit Stoke Moran that day; she gathers her veil and glides out of the room.

sections.start_ref: The Adventure Of The Speckled Band ¶84
sections.end_ref: The Adventure Of The Speckled Band ¶94
sections.title: Holmes and Watson discuss the case; Roylott bursts in
sections.division_name: The Adventure Of The Speckled Band

moments.summary: Holmes and Watson sit by the fire talking through the case; the door crashes open and a huge, furious Roylott fills the doorway with his hunting-crop.

sections.start_ref: The Adventure Of The Speckled Band ¶95
sections.end_ref: The Adventure Of The Speckled Band ¶115
sections.title: Roylott's threats and Holmes's inquiry at Doctors' Commons
sections.division_name: The Adventure Of The Speckled Band

moments.summary: Roylott rages in the sitting-room, bends a steel poker in his hands and storms out while Holmes watches calmly.
Holmes straightens the poker back out and, at the table, reads Doctors' Commons notes on the will's figures.

sections.start_ref: The Adventure Of The Speckled Band ¶116
sections.end_ref: The Adventure Of The Speckled Band ¶126
sections.title: Journey through the Surrey lanes to Stoke Moran
sections.division_name: The Adventure Of The Speckled Band

moments.summary: Holmes and Watson ride in a trap through the Surrey lanes and approach the old Stoke Moran manor, where Helen waits at the stile.

sections.start_ref: The Adventure Of The Speckled Band ¶127
sections.end_ref: The Adventure Of The Speckled Band ¶140
sections.title: Examination of the outside of the wing and the shutters
sections.division_name: The Adventure Of The Speckled Band

moments.summary: Helen, joyful, learns of Roylott's trip to town; Holmes warns her and asks to see the rooms.
Holmes walks the ill-trimmed lawn studying the windows of the ruined wing, then tests the shutters and hinges from inside Helen's room.

sections.start_ref: The Adventure Of The Speckled Band ¶141
sections.end_ref: The Adventure Of The Speckled Band ¶157
sections.title: Inspection of Julia's bedroom: the bell-rope and ventilator
sections.division_name: The Adventure Of The Speckled Band

moments.summary: Holmes sits in the small whitewashed bedroom looking round at the bed, chest and bell-rope tassel lying on the pillow.
Holmes crawls on the floor with his lens, tugs the dummy bell-rope and studies the ventilator above the bed.

sections.start_ref: The Adventure Of The Speckled Band ¶158
sections.end_ref: The Adventure Of The Speckled Band ¶172
sections.title: Inspection of Roylott's chamber: safe, saucer and dog-lash
sections.division_name: The Adventure Of The Speckled Band

moments.summary: In Roylott's plainly furnished room Holmes examines the iron safe and the saucer of milk on top of it.
Holmes squats by the wooden chair and then lifts a dog-lash with a tied whipcord loop hanging from the bed corner.

sections.start_ref: The Adventure Of The Speckled Band ¶173
sections.end_ref: The Adventure Of The Speckled Band ¶194
sections.title: Holmes's plan for the night
sections.division_name: The Adventure Of The Speckled Band

moments.summary: On the lawn Holmes gives Helen his instructions for the night and she listens, hands clasped, in the grey afternoon light.

sections.start_ref: The Adventure Of The Speckled Band ¶195
sections.end_ref: The Adventure Of The Speckled Band ¶218
sections.title: Waiting at the Crown and the approach to the manor
sections.division_name: The Adventure Of The Speckled Band

moments.summary: From a window of the Crown Inn at dusk Holmes and Watson watch Roylott's trap drive past and the manor lamp light up.
In the inn's upper room Holmes and Watson talk by the window in gathering darkness, Holmes explaining the ventilator clue.
Holmes and Watson sit in the dark inn room with pipes, then set off into the night with the signal light ahead.

sections.start_ref: The Adventure Of The Speckled Band ¶219
sections.end_ref: The Adventure Of The Speckled Band ¶234
sections.title: The vigil in darkness
sections.division_name: The Adventure Of The Speckled Band

moments.summary: The two men leave the inn at night along a dark road, a single yellow light twinkling ahead through the gloom.
Crossing the moonless lawn toward the window, a strange deformed creature bolts from the laurels into the darkness.
Inside Helen's room in total darkness, Holmes and Watson sit by the bed, pistol and cane ready, listening.

sections.start_ref: The Adventure Of The Speckled Band ¶235
sections.end_ref: The Adventure Of The Speckled Band ¶246
sections.title: The snake, Roylott's death and its discovery
sections.division_name: The Adventure Of The Speckled Band

moments.summary: The two men wait in the dark room as the clock strikes the hours and a lantern's gleam and burning-oil smell come through the ventilator.
Holmes strikes a match and lashes his cane at the bell-pull while a terrible cry rings through the house.
Holmes and Watson enter Roylott's chamber with a lantern, finding the doctor dead in his chair, a yellow speckled band around his head.
A swamp adder rears from Roylott's hair; Holmes seizes it with the dog-lash and thrusts it into the iron safe.

sections.start_ref: The Adventure Of The Speckled Band ¶247
sections.end_ref: The Adventure Of The Speckled Band ¶251
sections.title: Aftermath and Holmes's explanation
sections.division_name: The Adventure Of The Speckled Band

moments.summary: Aftermath summarized: Helen is taken to Harrow and the inquest rules the death an accident with a pet.
On the train home Holmes explains his reasoning to Watson, the two talking seated across from each other in the carriage.

sections.start_ref: The Adventure Of The Engineer’S Thumb ¶1
sections.end_ref: The Adventure Of The Engineer’S Thumb ¶6
sections.title: Watson is woken by the guard
sections.division_name: The Adventure Of The Engineer’S Thumb

moments.summary: Watson in his dressing gown at the top of his stairs while the railway guard, by the consulting-room door, whispers that he has brought a new patient.

sections.start_ref: The Adventure Of The Engineer’S Thumb ¶7
sections.end_ref: The Adventure Of The Engineer’S Thumb ¶15
sections.title: Hatherley's arrival and hysteria
sections.division_name: The Adventure Of The Engineer’S Thumb

moments.summary: Watson in his consulting room with a pale young man in heather tweed, his bloodstained handkerchief wrapped around one hand, who laughs hysterically before being steadied with brandy.

sections.start_ref: The Adventure Of The Engineer’S Thumb ¶16
sections.end_ref: The Adventure Of The Engineer’S Thumb ¶39
sections.title: The wound is dressed and the pair go to Holmes
sections.division_name: The Adventure Of The Engineer’S Thumb

moments.summary: The young man unwinds his handkerchief to show the mutilated hand with its thumb torn away, and Watson sponges, cleans and bandages the bloody wound.
Watson and the patient, now revived, talk of the attack as they prepare to leave, and Watson hurries upstairs to fetch his wife before the two ride off in a hansom.

sections.start_ref: The Adventure Of The Engineer’S Thumb ¶40
sections.end_ref: The Adventure Of The Engineer’S Thumb ¶44
sections.title: Breakfast at Baker Street
sections.division_name: The Adventure Of The Engineer’S Thumb

moments.summary: Holmes in a dressing gown in his Baker Street sitting room, serving breakfast and settling the injured visitor on a sofa with a pillow and brandy while Watson watches.

sections.start_ref: The Adventure Of The Engineer’S Thumb ¶45
sections.end_ref: The Adventure Of The Engineer’S Thumb ¶87
sections.title: Stark's commission in Victoria Street
sections.division_name: The Adventure Of The Engineer’S Thumb

moments.summary: In Hatherley's sparse Victoria Street office, the thin, pale Colonel Stark stands at the door eyeing the young engineer suspiciously and demanding his promise of secrecy.
Stark springs to the open door to check the empty passage, then draws his chair close and fixes Hatherley with a hard, questioning stare.
Stark offers fifty guineas for a night's work at Eyford and explains the fuller's-earth scheme while Hatherley listens and then leaves the office.

sections.start_ref: The Adventure Of The Engineer’S Thumb ¶88
sections.end_ref: The Adventure Of The Engineer’S Thumb ¶96
sections.title: The night drive to Eyford
sections.division_name: The Adventure Of The Engineer’S Thumb

moments.summary: A chestnut carriage waits in the dark at Eyford station, and Hatherley is hurried inside by a silent man and driven along jolting country roads.

sections.start_ref: The Adventure Of The Engineer’S Thumb ¶97
sections.end_ref: The Adventure Of The Engineer’S Thumb ¶112
sections.title: Arrival and the woman's warning
sections.division_name: The Adventure Of The Engineer’S Thumb

moments.summary: A pretty woman in a rich dark dress holds up a lamp in a dim hallway as Stark whispers to her, then Stark shows Hatherley into a plain room with German books.
The frightened woman slips into the quiet room, pleads with Hatherley in broken English to leave, and then vanishes as footsteps approach on the stairs.
Stark and a stout, bearded manager named Ferguson lead Hatherley up through a decaying labyrinth of corridors to the machine room.

sections.start_ref: The Adventure Of The Engineer’S Thumb ¶113
sections.end_ref: The Adventure Of The Engineer’S Thumb ¶121
sections.title: Trapped in the hydraulic press
sections.division_name: The Adventure Of The Engineer’S Thumb

moments.summary: Hatherley crouches inside the small iron-floored chamber of the hydraulic press, examining the leaking cylinder by lamplight.
Stark looks down at Hatherley scraping the trough, then slams the little door shut and turns the key in the lock.
The black iron ceiling descends slowly toward a terrified Hatherley, who claws at the locked door in the lamplight as the engine clanks.

sections.end_ref: The Adventure Of The Engineer’S Thumb ¶133
sections.title: Escape through the window and recovery in the garden
sections.division_name: The Adventure Of The Engineer’S Thumb

moments.summary: Hatherley squeezes through a hidden panel in the wooden wall into a dim stone corridor, where the woman kneels beside him holding a candle.
The woman urges Hatherley toward a moonlit bedroom while Stark charges down the passage with a lantern and a cleaver, and Hatherley climbs onto the window sill.
Stark shoves past the woman, who clings to him, and swings his cleaver at Hatherley hanging from the sill, who falls into the moonlit garden.
Hatherley staggers through the rose bushes, sees his bleeding thumb, and then collapses in a faint beside the hedge at dawn.
Hatherley, bloodied and dazed, questions a porter at the morning station about a carriage and Colonel Stark, the porter shaking his head.

sections.start_ref: The Adventure Of The Engineer’S Thumb ¶134
sections.end_ref: The Adventure Of The Engineer’S Thumb ¶160
sections.title: Holmes reads the advertisement and the party heads for Eyford
sections.division_name: The Adventure Of The Engineer’S Thumb

In a train carriage, the inspector spreads a county map and draws a circle, while the four men each name a different direction.
Holmes points to the centre of the map circle, and then the party sees a column of smoke rising over trees as the train reaches Eyford.

sections.end_ref: The Adventure Of The Engineer’S Thumb ¶176
sections.title: The burning house and the aftermath
sections.division_name: The Adventure Of The Engineer’S Thumb

Hatherley and Holmes ride back to London in a train carriage, Hatherley lamenting his lost thumb and fee while Holmes laughs and calls it experience.

sections.start_ref: The Adventure Of The Noble Bachelor ¶1
sections.end_ref: The Adventure Of The Noble Bachelor ¶16
sections.title: Lord St. Simon's letter and the newspaper cuttings
sections.division_name: The Adventure Of The Noble Bachelor

moments.summary: A reflective narrator, Watson, in an upper-class setting: the St. Simon affair fades from society gossip, though he will sketch it now.
Watson lounges in an armchair in rainy Baker Street, legs up, newspapers strewn about, a noble crest envelope lying on the table.
Holmes enters and opens the crested letter at the table; he and Watson banter about its professional, noble origin.
Holmes asks Watson to turn over newspapers while he reads the letter aloud, Watson sitting in the armchair among the clippings.

sections.start_ref: The Adventure Of The Noble Bachelor ¶17
sections.end_ref: The Adventure Of The Noble Bachelor ¶45
sections.title: Holmes reads the notice and the newspaper account
sections.division_name: The Adventure Of The Noble Bachelor

moments.summary: Holmes reads the letter aloud and inspects the ink smear on the sheet, glancing at the clock showing three.
Holmes takes a red reference volume from the shelf by the mantelpiece and reads the peerage entry while Watson sorts clippings.
Watson reads the society column about the American heiress's marriage; Holmes stretches his legs toward the fire, yawning.
Watson lists the wedding notices, and Holmes sits upright when told the bride vanished at the wedding breakfast.
Watson reads the morning paper account of the wedding; a bell rings at the door as the clock passes four.

sections.start_ref: The Adventure Of The Noble Bachelor ¶46
sections.end_ref: The Adventure Of The Noble Bachelor ¶80
sections.title: Lord St. Simon's first interview
sections.division_name: The Adventure Of The Noble Bachelor

moments.summary: Lord St. Simon enters, pale and stooped with grizzled hair and dandyish dress, swinging his eyeglasses; Holmes rises to greet him.
Holmes and the nobleman exchange clipped remarks by the fire about past clients, the nobleman seated in a basket chair.
Holmes questions the nobleman briskly about how he met the bride in America and her father's wealth.
The nobleman describes his wife's character and opens a locket to show her ivory miniature; Holmes studies it closely.

sections.start_ref: The Adventure Of The Noble Bachelor ¶81
sections.end_ref: The Adventure Of The Noble Bachelor ¶110
sections.title: The wedding morning and the maid
sections.division_name: The Adventure Of The Noble Bachelor

moments.summary: Holmes asks about the wedding day; the nobleman recalls his bride's cheerfulness and first hints of temper.
The nobleman recounts the dropped bouquet and a gentleman in a pew who returned it, in the church setting.
At the Doran house, the bride speaks in hushed tones with her American maid Alice, mentioning 'jumping a claim'.
The bride walks alone into the breakfast room, then hurriedly leaves the table and never returns.

sections.start_ref: The Adventure Of The Noble Bachelor ¶111
sections.end_ref: The Adventure Of The Noble Bachelor ¶128
sections.title: Flora Millar and the disturbance at the house
sections.division_name: The Adventure Of The Noble Bachelor

The nobleman describes Flora Millar's past at the Allegro and her disturbance at the door, with police men nearby.
Holmes asks whether the nobleman could see out of the window from the breakfast table; the Park is visible.

sections.start_ref: The Adventure Of The Noble Bachelor ¶129
sections.end_ref: The Adventure Of The Noble Bachelor ¶141
sections.title: Holmes's conclusions and Lord St. Simon's departure
sections.division_name: The Adventure Of The Noble Bachelor

moments.summary: Holmes says he is done questioning; the nobleman rises, and Holmes claims he has already solved it.
The nobleman demands where his wife is; Holmes says he will supply the detail, and the nobleman bows out stiffly.

sections.start_ref: The Adventure Of The Noble Bachelor ¶142
sections.end_ref: The Adventure Of The Noble Bachelor ¶158
sections.title: Lestrade arrives with the wedding clothes
sections.division_name: The Adventure Of The Noble Bachelor

moments.summary: Lestrade sits, wet and nautical, complaining of the case as Holmes watches him with a twinkle.
Lestrade admits he has been dragging the Serpentine for the bride's body; Holmes laughs and mocks the search.
Lestrade opens his canvas bag and spills a wet wedding dress, satin shoes, and veil onto the floor.

sections.start_ref: The Adventure Of The Noble Bachelor ¶159
sections.end_ref: The Adventure Of The Noble Bachelor ¶178
sections.title: The note and the hotel bill
sections.division_name: The Adventure Of The Noble Bachelor

moments.summary: Holmes rebukes Lestrade's reasoning as Lestrade insists the dress implicates Flora Millar.
Lestrade produces a card-case note from the dress pocket and slaps it on the table in front of Holmes.
Holmes examines the note and turns the paper over, catching his eye on a fragment of hotel bill on the reverse.
Lestrade protests that the wrong side is up and reads the hotel bill aloud; Holmes insists it matters.

sections.start_ref: The Adventure Of The Noble Bachelor ¶179
sections.end_ref: The Adventure Of The Noble Bachelor ¶186
sections.title: Lestrade leaves and the supper arrives
sections.division_name: The Adventure Of The Noble Bachelor

moments.summary: Lestrade departs with a look of despair and a gesture, and Holmes puts on his overcoat as a confectioner's man lays out a cold supper.
Holmes returns at nine, sees the supper laid for five, and hears Lord St. Simon's footsteps on the stairs.

sections.start_ref: The Adventure Of The Noble Bachelor ¶187
sections.end_ref: The Adventure Of The Noble Bachelor ¶200
sections.title: Lord St. Simon meets Hatty and Frank
sections.division_name: The Adventure Of The Noble Bachelor

moments.summary: Lord St. Simon bursts in, glasses swinging, agitated, and sinks into a chair with his hand to his forehead.
Lord St. Simon frets about the family's humiliation as Holmes opens the door to the American couple.
Hatty steps toward Lord St. Simon, who stands rigid with his hand in his coat; she pleads with him.

sections.start_ref: The Adventure Of The Noble Bachelor ¶201
sections.end_ref: The Adventure Of The Noble Bachelor ¶210
sections.title: Hatty tells her story
sections.division_name: The Adventure Of The Noble Bachelor

moments.summary: Lord St. Simon bitterly refuses apology while Holmes offers to leave the room; the American husband speaks up.
Hatty recounts the old mining-camp romance with Frank, the engagement and her father's disapproval.
Hatty describes hearing Frank was killed by Apaches and her long grief, then her London engagement.
At the altar, Hatty sees Frank in the first pew; he signals her to be still and passes a note.
Hatty recalls slipping out after Frank, a cab ride, and lodgings in Gordon Square where the couple reunited.
Frank explains how he read the wedding notice, and Hatty explains the bundle of clothes dropped away and her shame.

sections.start_ref: The Adventure Of The Noble Bachelor ¶211
sections.end_ref: The Adventure Of The Noble Bachelor ¶217
sections.title: Lord St. Simon leaves and the supper
sections.division_name: The Adventure Of The Noble Bachelor

Holmes greets Frank warmly, speaking of Anglo-American kinship as the two stand in the lamplit room.

sections.start_ref: The Adventure Of The Noble Bachelor ¶218
sections.end_ref: The Adventure Of The Noble Bachelor ¶226
sections.title: Holmes explains his reasoning
sections.division_name: The Adventure Of The Noble Bachelor

moments.summary: After the visitors leave, Holmes explains the case's simplicity; Watson asks whether Holmes himself erred.
Holmes traces his chain of deduction by the fire, showing how the bride's conduct revealed a previous husband.
Holmes describes tracing the hotel bill and the couple's Gordon Square address through the hotel registers.
Watson remarks on Lord St. Simon's ungracious manner; Holmes smiles and reaches for his violin by the fire.

In the sitting room the distraught visitor beats his head against the wall, and Holmes soothes him into the easy-chair before he gives his name, Alexander Holder of the banking firm.

The nobleman leans across the banker's desk, stressing the coronet's value and urging discretion as he hands it over.

sections.end_ref: The Adventure Of The Beryl Coronet ¶44
sections.title: The coronet taken home to Streatham

sections.title: Household details and the night's warnings

sections.division_name: The Adventure Of The Beryl Coronet

Mary faints in the bedroom doorway at the sight of the coronet as the police inspector and constable enter the house and Arthur is taken into custody.

sections.title: Questioning the banker at Baker Street
sections.division_name: The Adventure Of The Beryl Coronet

sections.end_ref: The Adventure Of The Beryl Coronet ¶106
sections.title: Plan to visit Streatham

sections.end_ref: The Adventure Of The Beryl Coronet ¶146
sections.title: Questions to Mary and the coronet examined
sections.division_name: The Adventure Of The Beryl Coronet

sections.start_ref: The Adventure Of The Beryl Coronet ¶147
sections.end_ref: The Adventure Of The Beryl Coronet ¶166
sections.title: Holmes examines the grounds and departs

sections.end_ref: The Adventure Of The Beryl Coronet ¶176

brief.tone: Quiet, foggy domestic unease in London giving way to a sunny but menacing Hampshire countryside, ending in a sudden violent climax; restrained Victorian detective mood rather than gothic excess.
depiction_rules: Show the mastiff's attack only at the end, and keep Rucastle's wounds offstage or lightly suggested rather than graphic.
Do not depict Alice Rucastle's imprisonment in detail; the barricaded room may be shown empty or dim with the bed and linen.
Violet's cut hair may be shown as short and the electric-blue dress as worn but well-fitted.
Holmes is shown in his Baker Street manner with pipe and dressing-gown contexts as appropriate; avoid anachronistic gadgets.
Show the copper beeches as a dark-leafed group of trees before a whitewashed house.

cast.note: The God of Israel in Exodus (burning bush, plagues, law) and in 1 Samuel (Hannah, Samuel, the ark); the same deity across both books.

cast.name: Amalekites
cast.note: The people who attack Israel at Rephidim in Exodus and raid Ziklag in 1 Samuel; the same people across both books.

cast.note: Hebrew leader raised in Pharaoh's house, son of a Levite mother; flees to Midian, then leads Israel out of Egypt and receives the law at Sinai.

cast.note: Moses' elder brother and spokesman; becomes the first high priest and makes the golden calf.

brief.tone: Awe and sacred dread in the plague and mountain scenes, grief and tension in the flight, and warm, devotional calm in the craft and law passages.
depiction_rules: Yahweh is never given a human face or full body; show him as a voice, a burning bush, a pillar of cloud or fire, or the glory filling the tabernacle.
Moses' face shines after Sinai; render as a radiance or veil rather than a literal glow.
The plagues are shown as they occur in the text, with the river blood, swarms, hail, locusts, and darkness, without gratuitous gore beyond the death of the firstborn.
The golden calf is an idol to be shown as a molten calf, not as a god.
The Passover blood on doorposts is shown on lintel and posts only.
Laws and ritual instructions can be shown as objects and settings, not as literal legal scenes.

era.name: Late Bronze Age Egypt, Sinai, and the Sinai wilderness
era.people: Egyptians with shaven heads, linen kilts and wigs, and Hebrew clans in simple desert clothing, dark-haired and bearded; Midianite shepherds.
era.dress: Linen kilts and tunics for Egyptians; plain woven wool and linen for Israelites; priestly garments of blue, purple, scarlet and gold-threaded linen with an ephod, breastplate and bells.
era.buildings_and_objects: Brick storage cities such as Pithom and Raamses for Pharaoh; tents and a portable tabernacle with acacia boards, gold-overlaid ark, lampstand, altars and bronze court; papyrus baskets, clay kneading troughs, rods and staves.
era.technology: Brickmaking with straw and mortar, chariots and horses in the Egyptian army, bronze and gold metalwork, weaving and embroidery, fire and oil lamps; no iron tools, writing on stone tablets, and no coinage (weights are used).

brief.tone: Austere, tense and intimate: a book of prophecy, kingship and fraught loyalty, with grief and dread in quiet interiors and bursts of violence on open fields.
depiction_rules: Yahweh is never shown in human or animal form; depict only effects (a voice, light, thunder, the ark) rather than a visible deity.
The ark of the covenant may be depicted as a gold-covered chest with cherubim, not as a person.
Dagon, the Ashtaroth and the teraphim are idols and may be shown as statues without divine presence.
The Philistine champion Goliath is a fully armed giant; the raw violence of the sling stone and beheading may be shown but without gratuitous gore.
The Woman of Endor's necromancy is shown with Samuel as an old robed figure rising from the ground, not as a dramatic demonic spectacle.
Nudity (Saul prophesying naked, 19:24) may be depicted with restraint.

era.name: Late Bronze to early Iron Age Israel and Philistia, c. 11th century BCE
era.people: Israelite tribes (Ephraimites, Benjamites, Judahites) living as farmers and herders in hill country; Philistines as an organized city-state people with bronze and iron weapons; neighbors include Ammonites, Moabites, Amalekites and Edomites.
era.dress: Linen ephods for priests and boys; robes and mantles for elders and kings; bronze helmets and coats of mail for warriors; shepherds' bags and slings; simple woven tunics for common people.
era.buildings_and_objects: Mud-brick and stone houses with flat roofs; the tabernacle at Shiloh with doorposts and gates; altars of stone; the wooden ark overlaid with gold; threshing floors; watchtowers and strongholds; caves used as refuges.
era.technology: Bronze and emerging iron weapons and tools (iron spearheads, blacksmiths are rare among Israel); chariots and horses used by Philistines; oil lamps and horns for anointing; no writing of a full literary kind beyond scribal notes, but a book of royal law is written.

brief.tone: Reverent, quiet and luminous: intimate household scenes beside public crowds, with angelic light and dusk over Jerusalem, and grief giving way to hope.
depiction_rules: Show Jesus as a human figure without a fixed face-type rule beyond the era's appearance; avoid halos unless the scene demands a glory motif.
The divine voice and angels should appear through light, cloud, and posture rather than literal flesh where possible.
Satan and demons may be shown as dark or distorted presences, not as detailed monsters.
Violence (the crucifixion, the beheading referred to by Herod) is restrained and not gratuitous.
Women are present throughout and should be drawn as full participants, including in the nativity, the healing, and the resurrection.
Avoid depicting Jesus' mother with a mother-and-child emphasis that goes beyond the text.

brief.tone: Contemplative and luminous, with a sense of divine glory breaking into ordinary life; quiet intimacy in dialogue scenes and tension in conflict scenes.
depiction_rules: Depict Jesus as a Jewish man of the 1st century, not with the halo-and-blue-robe stereotype of later art unless the illustration calls for it.
Show the divine voice from the sky and the angels in white as light rather than as human figures where possible.
Handle the crucifixion with restraint, avoiding gratuitous gore while keeping its weight.
Do not depict God the Father in human form.
Show the Holy Spirit as a dove or as wind/breath only where the text names it.
Avoid caricaturing Jews, Pharisees and Judas; depict the opponents as religious authorities and crowds with individual dignity.

era.name: Roman Judea and Galilee, c. AD 30
era.people: Jewish villagers, fishermen, priests, Pharisees, Samaritans, Roman soldiers and officials; mostly brown-skinned Mediterranean people with dark hair and beards for men.

era.buildings_and_objects: Stone houses with flat roofs, village wells, stone water jars, the Jerusalem temple and its courts, synagogues, rock-cut tombs closed by a rolled stone, lamps, nets and boats on the Sea of Galilee, olive groves and vineyards.
era.technology: Oil lamps, torches, handmade boats and nets, hand-milled grain and baked bread, wine and oil; no photography, no printed books, no firearms, no clocks; Roman roads and governor's praetorium exist.

brief_flags.text: Depict Jesus as a Jewish man of the 1st century, not with the halo-and-blue-robe stereotype of later art unless the illustration calls for it.
Avoid caricaturing Jews, Pharisees and Judas; depict the opponents as religious authorities and crowds with individual dignity.
